overview: This file documents U.S. diplomatic and consular engagement with Japanese rules governing foreign entry, visas, temporary landing, residence, employment, transit, registration, travel, and deportation, chiefly during the 1930s. It combines routine traveler inquiries and individual disputes with extensive translations and legal analysis of Japan’s 1939 alien-control ordinance. Major subjects include reciprocal visa-fee arrangements, documentation requirements for military personnel and ship passengers, the treatment of entertainers and other foreign workers, possible discrimination against German Jews, restrictions affecting Chinese residents of Taiwan, and treaty-rights questions. The file also contains a substantial report—with statistics and organizational regulations—on Japan’s state-supported campaign to develop foreign tourism, plus later administrative circulation slips.
interest: The file is especially valuable for showing how migration control operated through both formal law and discretionary administrative practice. The Marcus Show controversy, cases involving travelers without passports, and consular guarantees reveal how misunderstandings, fees, politics, and cultural objections could determine whether foreigners were admitted or allowed to remain. The two translations and accompanying legal assessments of the 1939 ordinance provide unusually detailed evidence of Japan’s expanding surveillance and regulation of aliens on the eve of the Pacific War. The tourism report offers a useful counterpoint: Japan was simultaneously promoting foreign visitors for economic and diplomatic purposes while tightening the machinery used to monitor and restrict them.
